Vignette: Amara

Amara is sixty-three years old, a woman who carries herself with a quiet, deliberate composure that colleagues in her financial analysis firm have long mistaken for confidence. She arrived in the country twenty-one years ago from the Democratic Republic of Congo, having fled with her two youngest children through three borders over the course of eleven days. She does not often speak about what happened during those eleven days. When she does, it is in fragments — a sentence here, a silence there — as though the full story, spoken aloud, might break something that she has spent two decades carefully holding together.

The journey began after soldiers came to her neighborhood in Kinshasa. She had been a mid-level accountant at the time, a woman with a tidy apartment and a routine she trusted. Within forty-eight hours, that routine was gone. She witnessed her neighbor shot in the street. She walked past bodies she did not look at directly, because she understood even then that looking would mean carrying them forever. She hid her children under the floor of a truck. She traded her wedding ring for safe passage across one border and her mother's gold earrings for passage across another. By the time she reached the refugee camp, she had not slept in five days.

Now she sits in a high-rise office and builds financial models. Her work is meticulous — her supervisor has called her the most precise analyst on the floor — and she understands, without quite naming it, that precision is the thing that keeps her anchored. Numbers behave. Numbers do not surprise you in the middle of the night.

But nights are where Amara lives a different life entirely. She rarely sleeps more than three hours before waking, heart hammering, certain that she has heard something outside the door. She gets up, checks the locks — the front door, the balcony, the windows — and then sits in the kitchen under the overhead light until the sky begins to lighten. She has done this for years. She thinks of it simply as her schedule.

During the day, certain things reach her without warning. The sound of a car backfiring on the street below her office sends her body into a state her mind cannot immediately explain. She grips the edge of her desk and breathes until the sensation passes, then returns to her spreadsheet as though nothing happened. A news broadcast showing displaced people — anywhere in the world, any conflict — requires her to leave the room. She does not watch the news anymore. She has not watched it in over a decade.

Amara has been single since arriving in the country. She maintains warm but careful relationships with her adult children, who live nearby and worry about her in ways she gently deflects. She attends church on Sundays, where she sits near the exit. She has a small group of Congolese friends with whom she shares meals and sometimes laughter, but there is a layer of her experience she has never shared with any of them — not the bodies in the street, not the sound the truck made when the soldiers walked around it, not the particular quality of her children's silence as they lay hidden beneath the floor.

She describes herself as a private person. She describes the past as the past. But lately she has noticed that the distance she once maintained between then and now has been narrowing. A young Congolese woman joined her office last month, and something about the woman's accent — warm, familiar, musical — has been opening doors inside Amara that she thought she had sealed. She finds herself sitting at her desk with tears on her face and no memory of when they started. She finds herself wondering, for the first time in years, whether carrying this alone is something she can continue to do.
